analysis.one_liner: Phases in overtime pay for farm workers and strips away federal wage and hour exemptions for agricultural labor.
analysis.headline: Introduced on August 6, 2026, with 13 Democratic and one Independent cosponsor, the bill was referred to the Senate labor committee and has received no hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal wage law has long exempted agricultural workers from the overtime rules that cover most other jobs, and carries extra carve-outs for certain farm work. This bill phases in time-and-a-half pay for farm workers who work more than 55 hours a week starting in 2027, tightening each year until the threshold reaches the standard 40 hours. It also narrows the agricultural exemptions so they cover only an employer's immediate family, repeals several exemptions for specific kinds of farm work, and gives the smallest farms more years to comply.
analysis.who_benefits: Farmworkers — including migrant and seasonal workers, who make up a large share of the workforce — would gain the right to overtime pay after 55 hours a week in 2027 and after 40 hours by 2030 (later for farms with 25 or fewer employees). Workers in covered farm jobs would also gain minimum wage and child labor protections that currently do not apply to them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Farm workers, many working long harvest weeks

how_it_helps.text: Phases in overtime: employers of more than 25 farm workers must pay one-and-a-half times the regular rate for hours over 55 a week starting January 1, 2027, over 50 in 2028, over 45 in 2029, and over 40 from 2030 onward.
Gives the smallest farms — 25 or fewer employees — a later schedule: overtime rules begin January 1, 2030, and the 40-hour threshold is not reached until 2033.
Repeals the Fair Labor Standards Act provision (section 7(m)) that exempts many agricultural workers, including certain hand-harvest and range workers, from overtime pay.

Narrows the main agricultural exemption so it applies only to an employer's parent, spouse, child, or other immediate family member, and repeals a series of exemptions (sections 13(b)(12) through (16) and 13(h) through (j)) that deny minimum wage, overtime, and child labor protections to specified farm work.

analysis.who_pays: Agricultural employers — farms and the labor contractors who supply them — would pay higher payroll costs for overtime during long harvest weeks. Those costs could reach consumers through food prices or lead farms to cut hours or automate. The bill deliberately gives small farms years of lead time before the full rules apply.

drawbacks.text: The bill sets hard weekly hour thresholds, so a farm must either pay time-and-a-half or cap hours; during peak harvest, workers who want very long weeks may find them reduced instead.

Farms with 25 or fewer employees keep the current exemptions until 2030 and the full 40-hour threshold until 2033, so many of the smallest operations are spared the new rules for most of the phase-in.

Payroll costs rise for agricultural employers, and as with any wage mandate, employers can respond by reducing hours, raising prices, or shifting to machines — real trade-offs a supporter must acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is concrete and large for the workers affected: farm workers are among the lowest-paid workers in the country and today can be required to work 60- and 70-hour weeks with no overtime premium, a gap the bill closes on a fixed schedule. The costs fall on farms, concentrated in harvest season, and are buffered for small operations by the delayed timeline. The main design weakness is the long runway — workers at the smallest farms wait until 2033 for full protections, and the schedule gives employers years of certainty rather than forcing immediate adjustment. On balance the gains for workers outweigh the costs, though the transition is deliberately slow.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate's final session, sent to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on day one, and has sat there since with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Senator Alex Padilla introduced the Fairness for Farm Workers Act on August 6, 2026, with 13 cosponsors (12 Democrats and 1 Independent).
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and PENSIONS the same day; no further action appears on the record.
The bill amends the Fair Labor Standards Act to phase in overtime pay for agricultural workers beginning in 2027 and to repeal or narrow the law's agricultural exemptions.
Congress remains in session until January 3, 2027, so the bill is still technically alive, but no committee action has been scheduled.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, agricultural employers benefit: by keeping the bill bottled up in committee, they retain the current exemptions and continue to owe farm workers no overtime premium. Farm workers gain nothing yet.

for.name: Sen. Alex Padilla
for.role: U.S. Senator from California; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: 13 Senate cosponsors (12 Democrats, 1 Independent)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction, including Sanders, Warren, Booker, Schiff, Markey, Blumenthal, Van Hollen, Wyden, Cortez Masto, Rosen, Gallego, Alsobrooks, and Lujan.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions (majority-controlled)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on August 6, 2026, and has taken no action on it since — no hearing, no markup, no vote scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred, but all 14 sponsors are Democrats or an allied Independent and no Republican has cosponsored; with Republicans holding the Senate majority, the bill has not moved past referral.

industries.note: Employers of more than 25 farm workers would owe time-and-a-half after 55 hours a week starting in 2027 and after 40 hours from 2030, raising harvest-season labor costs. Their interest in keeping the current overtime exemption runs directly against farm workers' pay.
The bill does not spare them, only delays them: new overtime rules start in 2030 and the 40-hour threshold arrives in 2033. Until then they operate under the old exemptions.

industries.industry: Farm labor contractors and crew leaders
industries.note: The repeal of exemptions covering specified hand-harvest and other farm work removes carve-outs that contractors supplying those crews have relied on to pay without overtime or minimum wage protections.

analysis.trajectory: With only a few months left in the Congress, no Republican cosponsor, and no committee action since referral, the bill will almost certainly die in committee without a hearing or a vote — the usual fate for farmworker overtime bills introduced in the final session.
